source_text: πλὴν ἐν Χριστῷ, δι' ὕδατός τε καὶ αἵματος. Ἐξαριθμήσεται γὰρ ἑαυτῷ, φησὶν, ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας εἰς τὸν καθαρισμὸν αὐτοῦ, καὶ πλυνεῖ τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ, καὶ λούσεται τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ ὕδατι, καὶ καθαρὸς ἔσται. Καὶ τὸ μὲν εἰς ἑβδόμην ἡμέραν παρατείνεσθαι τὸν καθαρισμὸν, σημαίνει που πάντως, τὸ διὰ παντὸς τοῦ βίου, καὶ ἐν παντὶ τῷ τῆς ζωῆς χρόνῳ διασμήχεσθαι δεῖν ταῖς ἐπιεικείαις τοὺς ἐκ φαυλότητος κοσμικῆς μεταφοιτᾷν ἑλομένους ἐπὶ τὸ δρᾷν ἑλέσθαι τὰ πρεπωδέστερα. Τοιγάρτοι τῆς ἑβδομάδος μέτρον χρόνου πλήρωσιν ἔχει καὶ ἀνακύκλησιν εἰς τὸ ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, ὡς εἰς πέρας ἤδη καταίροντος τοῦ καιροῦ. Προσιέναι δὲ δεῖν καὶ ἀναγκαίως ἐπάγεσθαι ταῖς πρὸς ἡμῶν ἐπιεικείαις εὖ μάλα φησὶ, τὴν διὰ Χριστοῦ κάθαρσιν, καὶ τὸν δι' ὕδατος ἁγνισμὸν, ὡς ἐν ἀπονίψει σώματός τε καὶ ἱματίων νοουμένου λοιπὸν τοῦ ἁγίου βαπτίσματος, συνθέοντος δηλονότι καὶ τοῦ δι' αἵματος ἁγνισμοῦ. «Τῇ γὰρ ἡμέρᾳ, φησὶ, τῇ ὀγδόῃ, λήψεται ἑαυτῷ δύο τρυγόνας, ἢ δύο νεοσσοὺς περιστερῶν.» Κατασημήνειε δ' ἂν ἡ ἡμέρα πάλιν ὀγδόη τῆς μετὰ σαρκὸς οἰκονομίας ἡμῖν τὸν καιρὸν, ὅτε τὴν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ὑπέμεινε σφαγὴν ὁ Ἐμμανουὴλ, ἡ εὔγλωττος ἀληθῶς καὶ εὐηχεστάτη τρυγὼν, ἢ καὶ τῷ αἵματι τῷ ἰδίῳ τετελείωκεν εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς τοὺς ἁγιαζομένους. Ὅτι δὲ τὸ εὐῶδες ἅπαν ὁ Χριστοῦ θάνατος ἔχει (πέπρακται γὰρ ὑπὲρ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου ζωῆς, καὶ εἰς ἀναίρεσιν ἁμαρτίας), ἐμφήνειεν ἂν τὸ δύο μὲν εἶναι τὰς τρυγόνας, καταθύεσθαι δὲ μίαν μὲν ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτίας, εἰς ὁλοκαύτωμα δὲ τὴν ἑτέραν· ὅτι δὲ καὶ ἱλασμὸς ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν γέγονεν ὁ Χριστὸς, κατὰ τὰς Γραφὰς, παρέδειξεν εἰπών· «Καὶ ἐξιλάσεται περὶ αὐτοῦ ὁ ἱερεὺς ἔναντι Κυρίου ἀπὸ τῆς ῥύσεως αὐτοῦ.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Εὖ ἔφης. {ΚΥΡ.} Ὧδε μὲν οὖν τὸν γονοῤῥυῆ διακαθαίρεσθαι δεῖν, ὁ θεῖος ἡμῖν κατεχρησμῴδησε νόμος. Καταμιαίνει δὲ αὐτὸν, ᾧπερ ἂν γένοιτο καὶ ἀνεθέλητος ῥύσις, ἤγουν θελητὴ, καὶ πηγὴν ἔχουσα τὴν ἔμφυτον κίνησιν. Καὶ θελητὴ μὲν, ὡς ἐν ὁμιλίαις ταῖς πρὸς γυναῖκα, φημὶ, καὶ κατὰ νόμον τοῦ γάμου· ἀνεθέλητος δὲ αὖ, ὡς ἐν φαντασίαις τάχα που νυκτεριναῖς. Ἔφη γὰρ πάλιν ὡδί· «Καὶ ἄνθρωπος, ᾧ ἂν ἐξέλθῃ ἐξ αὐτοῦ κοίτη σπέρματος, καὶ λούσεται πᾶν τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ ὕδατι, καὶ ἀκάθαρτος ἔσται ἕως ἑσπέρας. Καὶ γυνὴ, ᾗ ἐὰν κοιμηθῇ ἀνὴρ μετ' αὐτῆς κοίτην σπέρματος, καὶ λούσονται τὰ σώματα ὕδατι, καὶ ἀκάθαρτοι ἔσονται ἕως ἑσπέρας.» Ἴσα γὰρ ἐπ' ἀμφοῖν τὰ ἐγκλήματα, καὶ τὸ παραλλάττον οὐδέν. Ἐν μὲν οὖν τῇ γονοῤῥοίᾳ, τὸ οἱονεὶ μακρόν πως ἡμῖν καὶ διηνεκὲς ἐγράφετο πάθος· ἐν δὲ τῷ προκειμένῳ, καταδηλοῦν ἔοικεν ὁ τοῦ νόμου σκοπὸς, ὡς ἔσται μεμολυσμένος καὶ εἰ μή τις τυχὸν τὴν εἰσάπαν καὶ ὁλόκληρον ἀῤῥωστοίη καταφθορὰν, ὁρῷτο δὲ πεπονθὼς, κἂν γοῦν ἐκ μέρους καὶ σπανιάκις. Τοιοῦτόν τι καὶ ὁ τοῦ Σωτῆρος ὑπέφηνε μαθητής· «Ὅταν γὰρ, φησὶν, ὅλον τὸν νόμον τελέσῃ τις, πταίσῃ δὲ ἐν ἑνὶ, γέγονε πάντων ἔνοχος. Ὁ γὰρ εἰπὼν, Μὴ μοιχεύσῃς, εἶπε καὶ, Μὴ φονεύσῃς. Εἰ δὲ οὐ μοιχεύσεις, φονεύσεις
pass_a_gloss: […] except in Christ, through water (hydōr) and blood (haima). 'He will count (exarithmēsetai) for himself seven days for his cleansing (katharismos), wash (plynei) his garments (himatia), bathe (lousetai) his body in water, and be clean (katharos)' (Lev 15:13 LXX). The cleansing being stretched (parateinesthai) to the seventh day signifies that through the whole life (bios), in all the time of living (zōē), those who chose to migrate (metaphoitan) from worldly baseness (phaulotēs kosmikē) to choosing to do the more fitting things must be scoured (diasmēchesthai) by acts of decency/good conduct (epieikeiai). For the week (hebdomas) as a measure of time has fulfilment (plērōsis) and recycling (anakyklēsis) to the beginning, as the season (kairos) already putting in (katairontos) at its end (peras). It says well that to our good conduct must come and be necessarily added (epagesthai) the cleansing (katharsis) through Christ and the purification (hagnismos) through water, holy baptism (baptisma) being understood in the washing (aponipsis) of body and garments, the purification through blood running together (syntheontos). 'On the eighth day he will take two turtledoves (trygones) or two young pigeons (neossoi peristerōn)' (Lev 15:14). The eighth day would mark (katasēmēneie) the time of the dispensation (oikonomia) with flesh, when Emmanuel, the truly eloquent (euglōttos) and most sweet-sounding (euēchestatē) turtledove, endured the slaughter (sphagē) for us, [who] by his own blood has perfected (teteleiōken) for ever (eis to diēnekes) those being sanctified (hagiazomenoi). That Christ's death has all fragrance (euōdes) — done for the life of the world and for the removal (anairesis) of sin — is shown by two turtledoves, one sacrificed (katathyesthai) for sin, the other for whole burnt offering (holokautōma); that Christ became propitiation (hilasmos) for our sins according to the Scriptures it showed by saying 'the priest will make atonement (exilasetai) for him before the Lord from his flow (rhysis)' (Lev 15:15). PALL.: Well said. CYR.: Thus the divine law oracled (katechrēsmōidēse) that the man with seminal flow (gonorrhyēs) must be cleansed. It defiles (katamiainei) also him to whom occurs a flow, involuntary (anethelētos) or voluntary (thelētē), having its source (pēgē) in the innate motion (emphytos kinēsis). Voluntary as in intercourse (homiliai) with a wife according to the law of marriage (gamos); involuntary as in nocturnal fantasies (phantasiai nykterinai). 'A man from whom goes out a lying of seed (koitē spermatos) will bathe all his body in water and be unclean till evening (hespera); and a woman with whom a man lies with a lying of seed, they will bathe their bodies in water and be unclean till evening' (Lev 15:16, 18). Equal the charges (enklēmata) on both, no difference (parallatton). In gonorrhoia a long and continuous suffering (pathos) was written; here the aim (skopos) of the law shows one will be defiled even if he does not suffer total and entire corruption (kataphthora), but is seen to have suffered even partly and rarely (spaniakis). The Savior's disciple hinted (hyphēne) the like: 'whoever fulfils the whole law but stumbles (ptaisēi) in one has become liable (enochos) of all. He who said Do not commit adultery also said Do not murder. If you do not commit adultery but murder […]' (Jas 2:10–11).
pass_b_english: Cyril: …except in Christ, through water and blood (1 John 5:6). For ‘he shall count for himself,’ it says, ‘seven days for his cleansing, and he shall wash his garments and bathe his body in water, and he shall be clean’ (Leviticus 15:13). That the cleansing is drawn out to the seventh day surely signifies that those who have chosen to pass from worldly baseness to the choice of doing what is more fitting must be scoured clean by good conduct throughout their whole life, at every moment they live. For the week, as a measure of time, holds completion and a circling back to the beginning, as when a period has already reached its end. And the law says very well that to our own good conduct there must come, as a necessary addition, the cleansing through Christ and the purification through water. For holy baptism is now understood in the washing of the body and the garments, and with it, clearly, goes the purification through blood. For ‘on the eighth day,’ it says, ‘he shall take for himself two turtledoves or two young pigeons’ (Leviticus 15:14). The eighth day, again, would signify for us the time of the dispensation in the flesh, when Emmanuel, the truly eloquent and most melodious turtledove, endured slaughter for us, and by his own blood has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). That Christ’s death is fragrant in every way (for it was accomplished for the life of the world (John 6:51) and for the abolishing of sin) would be shown by there being two turtledoves, one sacrificed for sin and the other as a whole burnt offering. And that, according to the Scriptures, Christ has become the atoning sacrifice for our sins (1 John 2:2), the law showed by saying: ‘And the priest shall make atonement for him before the Lord for his discharge’ (Leviticus 15:15).

Cyril: In this way, then, the divine law declared to us that the man with a discharge must be cleansed. But it also declares defiled the man who has an emission, whether involuntary or voluntary, springing from the natural impulse. Voluntary, I mean, as in relations with a wife according to the law of marriage; involuntary, again, as perhaps in dreams at night. For again it spoke thus: ‘And a man from whom an emission of seed goes out shall bathe his whole body in water, and he shall be unclean until evening. And a woman with whom a man lies with an emission of seed, they shall bathe their bodies in water, and they shall be unclean until evening’ (Leviticus 15:16, 18). For the charges against both are equal, and there is no difference. In the case of the discharge, then, the law described for us an affliction that was, as it were, long and continuous; but in the present case the aim of the law seems to make plain that a person will be defiled even if he does not suffer from complete and total corruption, but is seen to have suffered it only in part and rarely. The Savior’s disciple also hinted at something like this (James 2:10–11): ‘For whoever keeps the whole law,’ he says, ‘but stumbles in one point, has become guilty of all.
